meta.notes: Buckets from the series' verified choice-state list (TX + CT, ME, MA, NH, RI, NY, NJ, PA, MD, DE, OH, IL + DC). Notes marked verify:true need a fact-check pass before launch. Ramp validated on the sage surface: choice #1d6e56, hybrid #8bb296, monopoly = neutral #d8dbc9 (same convention as No RTO: pale means nothing to choose).

choice.label: You can pick
choice.body: People here can pick the company that sells them power, like picking a phone plan. The wires still belong to one company; the state checks those prices.

hybrid.label: In between
hybrid.body: Some people here can pick, but with big limits.

monopoly.label: One company
monopoly.body: One utility is the only choice. A state board checks its prices.

TX.note: Most Texans pick their power company. Areas served by co-ops, city utilities, and the parts of Texas outside ERCOT still have one company.

MD.note: A 2024 law capped prices and put new limits on sellers. Most sellers stopped offering home plans. A court fight over part of the law is still going.

MI.note: Michigan lets only 10% of its power load switch. That line is full. There is a waiting list to leave the utility.

CA.note: California opened its market in the 1990s, hit a crisis in 2000, and closed most of it. Many cities now team up to buy power for their residents instead.

NE.note: Nebraska is the only state where every utility is owned by the public.

NV.note: Big companies can pay a fee to leave the utility and buy power on their own. Homes cannot.

MT.note: Montana tried choice in the 1990s. Prices went up instead of down, and the state went back in 2007.

OR.note: The biggest business customers can shop. Homes cannot.

VA.note: Choice exists on paper for 100% renewable plans. The utilities' own green plans closed that door for homes. Only the very biggest power users can still shop.
